lines: Reliability Diagram on Your Own Model, taken apart.

beats.role_note: the stakes BEFORE the build begins — no terminal yet
beats.narration_text: You trained a classifier this week. It prints confidence scores. You have never checked whether those confidence scores mean anything. A model that says ninety-four percent and is right fifty-six percent of the time is not a reliable model — it's a confident wrong one. The reliability diagram makes your own overconfidence visible. And the shifted slice — the high-value subgroup the model matters most for — is where the decorative number gets caught.
beats.visual_intent: title card: 'your model says 94% — does it mean 94%?'; PROBLEM beat, no terminal yet

build.suggested: suggested prompt: You trained a classifier. It prints confidence scores. You have never checked whether those confidence scores mean anything.

beats.narration_text: In the terminal: ask Claude to write a script that loads your held-out predictions CSV — two columns, predicted probability and true label — bins into ten confidence bins, plots the reliability diagram against the perfect-calibration diagonal, computes ECE and Brier score, fits temperature scaling on a validation split, and re-plots. Then takes the subset of rows where feature X is above its median as a shifted slice and recomputes ECE on that slice. Print both ECE values.

props.command:
claude "Write a Python script that:
1. loads predictions.csv (predicted_prob, true_label)
2. bins into 10 confidence bins
3. plots reliability diagram vs diagonal
4. computes ECE and Brier score
5. fits temperature scaling on a val split, re-plots
6. takes rows where feature_x > median as
   'shifted slice', recomputes ECE
Print both ECE values: in-dist and shifted."

beats.role_note: terminal (Onda) — read the output before running
beats.narration_text: Read the three key operations before running. Calibration underscore curve from sklearn returns, per bin, the fraction of positives — the empirical positive rate — and the mean predicted probability. ECE is the mean absolute difference between those two. Temperature scaling fits a single scalar T on a validation split: T greater than one softens overconfident probabilities. And the shifted slice is the fairness-calibration intersection: does the model's overconfidence concentrate in the subgroup that matters most?

props.code:
# reliability_diagram.py — Claude Code output
from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve
import numpy as np

# ECE: mean absolute gap between predicted and empirical
ppv, mean_pred = calibration_curve(
    df["true_label"], df["predicted_prob"], n_bins=10
)
ece = float(np.mean(np.abs(ppv - mean_pred)))

# temperature scaling: T > 1 softens overconfidence
# optimized on held-out validation split
T = optimize_temperature(val_probs, val_labels)
scaled = sigmoid(logit(probs) / T)

# shifted slice: high-value subgroup
shifted = df[df["feature_x"] > df["feature_x"].median()]
ece_shifted = compute_ece(shifted)

beats.role_note: Manim animation: B04_ReliabilityDiagram — two panels side by side
beats.narration_text: Run it. Left panel: in-distribution reliability diagram. The curve tracks the diagonal reasonably well — ECE is point-zero-eight. Right panel: shifted slice, the high feature-X subgroup. The curve bends away from the diagonal at high confidence. ECE jumps to point-nineteen. The model that looks calibrated on its training distribution is systematically overconfident in the deployment regime it matters most for. That gap does not appear until you plot the shifted slice.
beats.visual_intent: Manim B04_ReliabilityDiagram: two reliability diagrams side by side — left (in-distribution, ECE=0.08, curve near diagonal) and right (shifted slice, ECE=0.19, overconfidence zone highlighted); ECE values animate in; a 'gap' arrow in the right panel

beats.role_note: terminal (Onda) — lock the prediction first, then apply temperature scaling
beats.narration_text: Before re-running with temperature scaling, lock a prediction. Ask Claude to add a step at the top of the script: prompt the user for their guessed ECE on the shifted slice, hash it, write it to predlock.log. Then run temperature scaling. After, resolve: print the guessed ECE, the actual ECE, and whether the hash still verifies. Calibration on training distribution does not survive a distribution shift — and the locked prediction is the only way to know whether you knew that.

props.command:
claude "Update reliability_diagram.py:
ADD at top: prompt user for guessed ECE on
shifted slice, hash+timestamp to predlock.log.
Apply temperature scaling, recompute shifted ECE.
AT END: print guessed ECE, actual ECE, the gap,
HASH VERIFIED / HASH MISMATCH."

beats.narration_text: Temperature scaling closes the in-distribution ECE gap — the curve moves to the diagonal. But on the shifted slice, ECE barely moves. Calibration on your training distribution does not survive a distribution shift. The reliability diagram is the instrument that makes your own overconfidence visible; the shifted slice is the test that exposes where it hides; and the prediction lock is the tool that prevents you from editing the guess after you see the result.
beats.visual_intent: recap card: 'temperature scaling: ECE in-dist closes; ECE shifted barely moves'; two ECE numbers side by side

build.suggested: suggested prompt: Temperature scaling closes the in-distribution ECE gap. On the shifted slice, ECE barely moves. Calibration doesn't survive a distribution shift.

beats.narration_text: Your move: take any model you shipped last week. Pull the held-out predictions — predicted probability and true label. Lock a guessed ECE before you run the script. Run the reliability diagram, then the shifted slice. If ECE rises on the shifted slice, you have a calibration problem in the regime that matters most — and you now have the number to report.
